activities.title: Visual Fraction Strips: Comparing Same-Size Wholes
activities.purpose: Remediate whole-number bias (M1) by visually demonstrating that dividing the same whole into more parts yields smaller individual pieces.
activities.instructions: Place two fraction strips of identical total length side-by-side. Cut strip A into 3 equal pieces (thirds) and strip B into 5 equal pieces (fifths). Observe that 1 third is noticeably longer than 1 fifth. Now highlight 2 thirds and 2 fifths: two thirds clearly covers more total length than two fifths.
activities.expected_learning_evidence: Learner acknowledges that cutting into more pieces makes each piece smaller, overriding whole-number comparison of denominators.

activities.title: Part-Size Explorer: Halves vs Eighths
activities.purpose: Remediate reversed denominator rule (M2) by showing that a larger denominator does not make a larger piece when the whole is fixed.
activities.instructions: Compare 1 slice of a pizza cut into 2 gigantic pieces (1/2) with 1 slice of the same pizza cut into 8 small pieces (1/8). Ask the learner: Would you rather have 1 slice from the pizza cut in 2 or 1 slice from the pizza cut in 8 if you want more pizza?
activities.visual_representation: [1/2 slice = 50% of whole] vs [1/8 slice = 12.5% of whole].
activities.expected_learning_evidence: Learner explains that dividing among more people (higher denominator) reduces each person's share.

activities.title: Common Denominator Grid
activities.purpose: Remediate numerator-only comparison (M3) by partitioning fractions to a shared common unit.
activities.instructions: When comparing fractions with different numerators and different denominators (like 3/7 vs 4/9), you cannot simply look at 3 vs 4 or 7 vs 9. Find a common denominator: 7 * 9 = 63. Convert 3/7 to 27/63 and 4/9 to 28/63. Now that unit sizes are identical (63rds), 28 parts is greater than 27 parts.
activities.expected_learning_evidence: Learner uses common denominator or benchmark reasoning rather than comparing numerators in isolation.

activities.title: Proportional Scaling vs Addition Explorer
activities.purpose: Remediate invalid equivalent-fraction transformation (M4) by contrasting multiplication with addition.
activities.instructions: Take fraction 1/2 (value 0.50). If you add 1 to top and bottom: (1+1)/(2+1) = 2/3 (value 0.67). Notice the value changed from 50% to 67%! Now multiply top and bottom by 2: (1*2)/(2*2) = 2/4 (value 0.50). Multiplying scales both parts equally because 2/2 = 1.
activities.visual_representation: Addition alters the ratio: 1/2 != 2/3. Multiplication preserves the ratio: 1/2 == 2/4.
activities.expected_learning_evidence: Learner demonstrates that equivalent fractions require proportional scaling (multiplication/division) by a non-zero factor.

activities.title: Calculation & Transcription Check
activities.purpose: Address arithmetic slip (S1) without assuming a conceptual misconception.
activities.instructions: Your mathematical logic was sound, but let's carefully check the arithmetic step. Re-calculate the multiplication or division step-by-step.
activities.visual_representation: Step 1: Check multiplication. Step 2: Verify simplification.
activities.expected_learning_evidence: Learner recalculates correctly and verifies their arithmetic.

activities.title: Reasoning Clarification Activity
activities.purpose: Collect evidence when student reasoning is ambiguous or missing (U1).
activities.instructions: Before we proceed, tell the tutor: What rule or mental picture did you use to choose that answer?
activities.visual_representation: Thinking bubble: Explain your step-by-step thinking.
activities.expected_learning_evidence: Learner provides explanatory text enabling classification.
